item.title: Eindhoven chip firm Euclyd raises €200m
item.description:
Eindhoven chip firm Euclyd raises €200m

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Eindhoven start-up Euclyd has raised more than €200 million to develop AI chips, and former ASML boss Peter Wennink has become chairman of the board, the company said on Tuesday.

The company is designing chips for what the industry calls inference, which is when an AI model is being used rather than trained. Most of that work is currently done on US-owned Nvidia processors. Euclyd says its chips will use less power and cost less.

Wennink was chief executive of ASML in Veldhoven from 2013 until 2024. In the statement he said Europe has “world-class capabilities across semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and systems engineering” and that Euclyd could build these into “a globally competitive AI infrastructure platform”.

Kastrup said in the same statement that the money would go on hiring engineers and speeding up development. “AI is becoming a foundation of economic growth, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness,” he said, “but its potential will remain constrained unless we fundamentally change the infrastructure beneath it.”

item.title: Scrap of 1700-year-old copy of The Odyssey washes up in Utrecht
item.description:
Scrap of 1700-year-old copy of The Odyssey washes up in Utrecht

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 1700-year-old scrap of parchment containing verses from the Odyssey has been discovered in the library of Utrecht University.

Researcher Mark de Kreij came across the fragile artefact two years ago while he was going through a collection of manuscripts that belonged to a German scientist.

The torn fragment measures just 6.6cm by 7.7cm, roughly the size of a playing card, and contains a handful of verses from book 12 of Homer’s epic work.

It describes the moment when Odysseus’s men kill and eat the sacred cattle of the sun god Helios, ignoring their leader’s warnings, which prompts Zeus to send a storm to destroy Odysseus’s fleet and kill his army.

De Kreij said the fragment had lain undetected in the library for years until he came across it while examining a collection of Coptic manuscripts that the university bought from a relative of the German academic Carl Schmidt.

The text, in ancient Greek, was nestled among a batch of Coptic papyri, Egyptian texts written in the Greek alphabet. It is thought to have been taken from a pocketbook edition produced in Egypt in the third or fourth century AD.

The university decided to publicise the discovery in the wake of the box-office success of Christopher Nolan’s recent screen adaptation, which has revived interest in The Odyssey and boosted sales of English and Dutch translations.

De Kreij, a lecturer in Ancient Greek, immediately recognised the verses when he came across the parchment. “Everbody who learns Greek learns Homer,” he told RTV Utrecht.

Enduring epic

Only a handful of fragments of copies of The Odyssey have survived from the period, but the discovery shows how the epic tale has endured and been passed down for millennia.

De Kreij said the fragment had probably survived because it comes from the midpoint of the book and so would have been protected by the outer pages.

“The strange thing about my job is that The Odyssey is about the least exciting thing you can find,” he said. “There are lots of boring passages in The Odyssey. But this is a great part.”

item.title: Ben Saunders, original winner of The Voice, found dead in lake
item.description:
Ben Saunders, original winner of The Voice, found dead in lake

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Ben Saunders, the winner of the first edition of TV talent show The Voice of Holland, has been found dead in a recreational lake near Arnhem.

Friends and family of the 43-year-old confirmed his death to the Telegraaf after police recovered a body from the Rijkerswoerdse Plassen at 1.20pm on Tuesday.

His brother, Dean, wrote in an Instagram post with a picture of himself and Ben as children: “My dear little brother died today. I have never felt such pain as I feel now. What a dreadful day for us all.”

Ben Saunders has not been formally identified, but he had several distinctive tattoos and was well known in the Gelderland biker community.

Police said his death was not being treated as a crime. Saunders had been reported missing earlier in the day.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dean Saunders (@deansaundersjr)

Saunders was born in London and moved to the Netherlands as a child with his English parents. He grew up in the Noord-Holland town of Hoorn before moving to Arnhem, where he opened a tattoo parlour.

His breakthrough came in 2011 when he won The Voice after dazzling judges with his rendition of the Kings of Leon song Use Somebody in his audition.

He and Dean, who won Popstars in the same year, had been entering TV talent shows for a decade, including the contest to represent the Netherlands in the 2003 Eurovision Song Contest. In the early 2000s they formed a band called Follow That Dream.

Ben’s winning song in The Voice, Kill for a Broken Heart, reached number 4 in the Dutch Top 40, while his first solo album, You Thought You Knew Me By Now, topped the charts on its release in April 2011.

Health and police troubles

But fame proved to be fleeting as Saunders began to struggle with his health and ran into trouble with the police. He had a spell in hospital with stomach pains and told the Telegraaf he had to use a stick on stage because he suffered from a hernia.

In 2016 he was given a community service sentence for abusing a traffic official and ordered to compensate a café owner for damaging his premises.

Saunders also turned out to be a member of the biker club Satudarah, which was banned in 2020 because of its extensive involvement in organised violence and drug dealing.

item.title: The speedy speech from the throne: What the papers say
item.description:
The speedy speech from the throne: What the papers say

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch papers found little to unite around in Tuesday’s king’s speech, with editorials picking at what was missing in substance and delivery.

The Volkskrant in its editorial remarked on the “lack of urgency” in the speech from the throne over measures to combat and alleviate climate change. Former climate minister turned prime minister Jetten’s green profile is “fading”, the paper wrote, as recent forecasts warn the Netherlands will come nowhere near realising its climate goals.

The less-than-emphatic reference to this year’s extreme temperatures in the king’s speech illustrates the prime minister’s wish to remain pals with everyone, by avoiding polarising issues, such as climate and a speedier energy transition, the paper said.

“Politicians too often believe that strict measures to protect the environment will weaken the country’s competitive strength but the reverse is the case in the long term,” it warned.

Trouw expressed surprise at the VVD’s stubborn and out-of-touch insistence on shielding the rich while raising taxes for everyone else when, according to a poll commissioned by the paper, voters across the board, including 50% of VVD voters, would support a rise in wealth tax.

“It is as if the VVD is fighting a rearguard battle over something a majority of voters want to get rid of, as economists and all manner of advisory commissions insist that it is wealth that should be taxed, not labour,” the paper wrote. “It will be up to the CDA and D66 to win that battle in the next few months.”

The Telegraaf commented on the fact that although the king’s speech contained few new measures, it was the longest in history, with 2,889 words, spoken in places at breakneck speed.

Fewer figures and less jargon went some way to make the speech more accessible and “the good news” was the king speedy delivery: an average of 2.5 words per second against his mother, former queen Beatrix’s, 1.6.

When the king mentioned the farmers and the “need for clarity regarding their long-term prospects,” they were actually setting fire to roads, “a standout moment”, the paper said.

The NRC, in its own analysis of the speech, has been totting up the number of times the word “cooperation” appeared. It’s 14, and that, the paper said, is a measure of how desperate this minority cabinet is to secure the support of the opposition both on the right and on the left.

The wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran are “only referred to halfway into the speech”, the paper noted, and while there is “violence” in Ukraine, the violence in Gaza and Iran is qualified as “a situation”.

In a scathing comment, the AD criticised the actions allegedly perpetrated by farmers during the king’s speech. “Those who want to save democracy don’t sabotage it”, the paper wrote.

“The most relevant passage in the speech was the one about polarisation. The one about the softer voice of people who are genuinely worried, which is increasingly being drowned out in the Netherlands.” The paper pointed out that sabotaging the railway system (which is still being investigated and has not been attributed to the farmers) comes with a penalty of 15-year prison sentence.

item.title: Texel police begin DNA testing for dozens of unidentified bodies
item.description:
Texel police begin DNA testing for dozens of unidentified bodies

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police in Texel are trying to identify the remains of 38 dead bodies who have washed ashore on the island between 1920 and 2010, all of which were buried anonymously. The first nine will be exhumed on Wednesday for DNA sampling.

It may take months to find matches and identify the bodies, police have said. Prior to 2010, it was not mandatory for authorities to check DNA bases in cases of missing identities and bodies were buried without sampling.

The first bodies being examined today were buried between 1940 and 1982 in the general cemetery in Den Burg. Some bodies were there long enough that new graves have been placed above them, regional broadcaster NH reported.

The exhumation follows years of pressure from the community in Urk, a former island and fishing town in Flevoland, where 31 fishermen were lost in the North Sea between 1922 and 1997 and never found. Their relatives hope DNA from the Texel graves will match their missing family members.

Texel council refused to open the graves for years, since the anonymous bodies lie among named graves still protected by burial rights, police spokesman Erwin Sintenie told NH.

The remains are also thought to include drowning victims and two Second World War naval air service scouts.

DNA testing has already solved several cases on the island. In 2020, a body that washed up in 1995 was identified as a 59-year-old Swedish sailor who had been missing for 25 years.

A 22-year-old Syrian who drowned in 2014 trying to swim the Channel and two Afghan men aged 20 and 27, whose remains washed up in 2023, have also been identified.

Sintenie said the number of anonymous dead on Texel is high compared with the rest of the country, possibly because of the strong currents around the island. Remains will be reburied immediately after sampling.

item.title: Ajax hit five for second match in a row to rise to fourth
item.description:
Ajax hit five for second match in a row to rise to fourth

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Ajax moved up to fourth place in the Eredivisie as they swept aside Willem II to notch up their second 5-1 victory in five days.

Oskar Gloukh and German veteran Julian Brandt combined to give the Tilburgers constant problems down the left channel, while Kasper Dolberg crowned a strong performance with the fifth goal.

The visitors, who ended AZ Alkmaar’s run of five straight wins at the weekend, held out until the 41st minute, when Davy Klaassen pounced on a loose ball after Brandt’s cross had opened up the defence.

The German doubled the score just before half-time before Gloukh took control after the break, setting up Viktor Tsyhankov for the third goal before getting on the scoresheet himself with a low shot beneath goalkeeper Maxime Delanghe.

Willem II pulled one back through Alessandro Ciranni, but Dolberg had the last word when he headed a cross against the post but managed to steer in the rebound.

Gloukh said his understanding with Brandt was helping to improve his game: “He’s a really good player with experience, you can learn from him in training and in the games. He understands me well even though we haven’t played much together.”

Ajax confirmed on Wednesday morning they had completed the signing of Malinese international Yves Bissouma, who was a free agent after being released during the summer by Tottenham Hotspur.

The 30-year-old played 202 games in the Premier League for Brighton & Hove Albion and Tottenham, but his career stalled in August 2024 when a film appeared on Snapchat of him inhaling nitrous oxide, also known as laughing gas, which is a controlled drug in the UK.

Director of football Jordi Cruyff said: “He can play in several positions and we are hoping to get him match fit as quickly as possible.”

Utrecht fans banned

Elsewhere, Utrecht have issued bans to 18 supporters after their home match against Go Ahead Eagles on September 5 was abandoned when fireworks and plastic cups were thrown from the stands.

Utrecht said the bans had been imposed after camera footage from the game was reviewed and further sanctions were likely.

“FC Utrecht is continuing to analyse the available images in order to identify others who were involved,” the club said in a statement.

The remaining 26 minutes were played in an empty stadium last Tuesday, with Go Ahead coming back from 3-1 down to draw 3-3.

item.title: Rail sabotage: farm activists suspected as police investigate
item.description:
Rail sabotage: farm activists suspected as police investigate

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police and the security service AIVD are investigating the widespread sabotage on train tracks throughout the centre and east of the Netherlands on Tuesday, which brought train services to a standstill for much of the day, amid reports that radical farmers’ protest groups were responsible.

Further disruptions on Tuesday evening continued after certain tracks, that had already been cleared, were again targeted, according to infrastructure company ProRail.

Sources told broadcaster NOS they had seen farmer groups discussing taking direct action on Prinsjesdag, including by fixing metal pipes to train lines. Doing this fools the system into thinking a train is already on the track and turns signals red.

A photo of a pipe fixed to a rail also circulated in online farmers’ groups, although it is not clear who took it or where, NOS reported. No arrests have been made and no group has claimed responsibility so far.

Justice minister David van Weel pledged to catch the culprits on Wednesday morning.

Farmers’ organisations have condemned the actions and said they had nothing to do with it. The Farmers Defence Force, responsible for recent motorway disruptions, said it was not responsible but that “wild actions” by individual farmers were expected on budget day in reaction to the government plans on nitrogen and livestock numbers.

Farming lobby LTO Nederland said the actions crossed a line. “Sabotage has nothing to do with the right to protest,” a spokesman told NOS. “Whoever is behind this should ask themselves seriously what interest is served by it.”

Farm protesters also set hay bales, tyres and pallets alight beside motorways including the A2 and A28, and police arrested 7 people near Breukelen. It is not known whether the same people were involved in the rail sabotage.

Police and intelligence officials have not yet commented on who they suspect is behind the actions, but sources did confirm to NOS that farmer protest groups were one scenario being considered.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said what happened went beyond all limits and created dangerous situations.

The disruptions coincided with Prinsjesdag, the state opening of parliament in the The Hague and the annual budget announcements.

Bart Schuurman, professor of terrorism and political violence at Leiden University, told NOS he expects public prosecutors to pursue serious charges. Deliberately endangering rail traffic carries a maximum sentence of 15 years, and potentially more if a court finds a terrorist motive. “Even if they were not consciously out to kill or injure anyone, they took the risk that trains would derail or collide,” he said.

item.title: The 2027 budget: the main measures and what it means for you
item.description:
The 2027 budget: the main measures and what it means for you

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The minority Dutch government published its 2027 budget on Tuesday, outlining the latest economic forecasts and its plans for the coming year. Here are the highlights:

Government and local government finances

  • Inflation will average 2.7% in 2027.
  • Wages will rise by an average of 3.8%.
  • Economic growth will remain in line with earlier projections at 1.2%, without major upsets.
  • The budget deficit will rise to 2.7%, well below the EU maximum of 3%.
  • The government plans to cut €400 million from spending on its own operations, with the aim of a structural reduction of €1 billion from 2030.
  • The local authorities fund will rise marginally to just under €50 billion, or €2,741 per resident.

Taxes

  • Spending power will fall marginally for all but pensioners and low-income households.
  • Plans to reform the Box 3 asset tax system are due in spring 2027.
  • Income tax in the first tax band (up to €39.20) will hit 36.23%, up from 35.75% now.
  • The income tax rate in the second tax band (up to €78,400) will rise from 37.56% to 38.16%
  • The arbeidskorting – a tax break for people in work – will rise slightly.
  • Employers will no longer be able to give workers a 20% discount tax free on the company’s own products.
  • The startersaftrek – a discount for the newly self-employed – will be cut to a nominal €10 in 2027 and scrapped altogether in 2028.
  • Untaxed travel expenses will rise to 25 cents per kilometre and has been backdated to the start of 2026.
  • BTW on plants, flowers and trips by balloon will rise from 9% to 21%.
  • Excise duty on alcohol will rise in line with inflation.

Defence and foreign affairs

  • €600 million extra will go to defence in 2027, taking the total to almost €29 billion, including €3.1 billion in military support for Ukraine.
  • €35 million will be spent on Dutch diplomatic missions abroad, partly offsetting cuts imposed by the last government. The consulate in Antwerp will remain open.
  • The development aid budget will rise by €400 million a year for the next three years, on top of the extra money agreed in June to win senate support and the partial reversal of the Schoof cabinet’s €2.4 billion cuts.
  • The Netherlands will not hit the OECD target of 0.7% of GDP on aid spending.

Benefits

  • Cuts to slash the period for claiming unemployment benefit from two to one year have been delayed until 2029.
  • A planned faster increase in the state pension age will not go ahead.
  • A lower maximum for payouts to pregnant women and people on invalidity benefit will not go ahead.
  • As announced earlier, low income households faced with mounting energy bills will be able to request help from a special energy fund

Healthcare

  • The health insurance own risk payment will rise from €385 to €400 in line with inflation.
  • €100 million is being allocated to ensure 60 to 69-year-olds can be vaccinated against shingles. The over 70s must pick up the bill themselves.
  • The government expects health insurance premiums will rise by €12.50 a month – although health insurance companies decide their own rates.

Housing and infrastructure

  • The housing ministry budget will top €7 billion next year.
  • Of this, €940 million will be allocated to boost major residential developments in terms of facilities and green spaces.
  • €630 million will go to specialised housing for the elderly.
  • From 2028, people who earn too much to live in rent-controlled homes will face bigger rent increases. The check will also include a look at individual assets.
  • Housing corporations will get a €425 million tax cut, allowing them to borrow an extra €6 billion to build social housing.
  • Private investors will be able to claim up to €10,000 for every mid-market rental home they build, from a budget of €500 million running from 2029 to 2033.
  • €1.5 billion has been allocated for road and bridge repairs until 2035.
  • €300 million will be invested annually in improving transport links to new residential developments, beginning in 2030.

Education and research

  • Education will get €668 million extra, largely reversing cuts to higher education imposed by the previous government.
  • There will be more investment in trade schools and in scientific research.
  • Funding is being set aside for the development of a national super computer and an Einstein telescope R&D centre.
  • The basic grant for students living away from home will rise by €50 from 2028.
  • €346 million will go to additional training for teachers from 2028.
  • More money will be allocated to help people shift into teaching from other professions.
  • €23 million is being allocated to provide free fruit in schools that request it.
  • The government will introduce a “sport pass” for 12 to 23-year-olds of €100 to €300 to be invested in sports.

Climate

  • Money will be allocated to help farmers who want to invest in making their businesses more sustainable and climate-friendly.
  • €1.3 billion is being allocated to store carbon dioxide in empty gas fields under the North Sea.
  • New measures to combat climate change will be announced in 2027.

Asylum and migration

  • The government says spending on refugees will reach €8 billion this year but go down to €5 billion by 2031 because of EU and other measures.
  • Local authorities which have not set up their own permanent refugee centres will be placed on a blacklist.
  • €22 million will be invested in setting up refugee centres outside the EU in 2027.
  • More money will be put into dealing with refugees who commit crimes and in secure accommodation for them.

Travel and transport

  • A 10 cent reduction in the price of diesel will be phased out from 2028 not 2027.
  • Tax on long-distance flights is being set at €59 instead of €74 to ensure Schiphol is not more expensive than German airports.

Royals

  • Spending on staff etc. will rise from €60.8 million to €62.1 million in 2027.
  • The king, queen and princess Amalia will have combined income of €2.7 million this year, but Amalia will not claim hers while she is studying.
  • The royals’ income rises in line with civil servant pay, which is 0.3% this year.

This article will be updated as more information becomes available.

item.title: Heinen warns “hard choices” are needed to secure future growth
item.description:
Heinen warns “hard choices” are needed to secure future growth

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Finance minister Eelco Heinen has said the Netherlands needs to build a “coalition for growth” to secure the future prosperity and security of the country.

Heinen said no one party had a monopoly on the answers and his own ideas on the role of markets and European co-operation had been forced to change in response to the challenges to the international order in recent years.

But he warned that the Netherlands also needed to cut its spending and reform social security and healthcare if it wanted to become “the best place to invest and grow”.

“International competition is becoming fiercer, our productivity is hardly growing and investment is lagging behind,” he said.

“Economic growth must become a national challenge, because a country that moves forwards is in everyone’s interest.”

Heinen, who represents the right-wing, fiscally conservative VVD party in the centre-right coalition, said the budget package had made space for the demands of opposition parties on both left and right.

Capital gains

Many of the original plans in the coalition agreement have been watered down or postponed as Heinen seeks support for a “common goal” that goes “beyond the next budget.”

The cabinet will bring forward plans to introduce capital gains tax system to replace the Box 3 asset tax, which the Supreme Court has said violates European human rights laws.

Heinen said the extended discount on fuel duty, cutting airport tax and making air travel more sustainable showed he was prepared to accommodate the wishes of opposition parties.

Social security

But his reference to “hard choices” were a clear signal that he is determined to press ahead with significant cuts to the social security and healthcare budgets, which the largest left-wing party Pro and the trade unions insist must be scrapped.

“Without reforms to social security and healthcare the money we spend today will hold back the growth of the future,” Heinen said.

The minister said the “handbrake” needed to be taken off investment, with the government increasing investment in helping startup businesses “get off the ground and stay here”.

Heinen said his ideas on international co-operation had changed in recent years as he saw the trend in the global economy turning from free trade to the agressive use of economic power.

European co-operation

“You know I believe strongly in the power of the market, but if the market comes up short and promising businesses can’t grow as a result, you have to be prepared to adapt your beliefs to reality,” he said.

International rules were no longer a guarantee of global security and the Netherlands needed to work on strengthening the European Union’s internal economic ties. “Yesterday’s world is not coming back,” he said.

“I will still be critical when Europa claims more influence than it needs or builds up more debts. But co-operation sometimes gives us more influence.

That’s why we must deepen European co-operation and make our internal market work better and improve our ties with countries outside Europe.”

item.title: Opposition parties dismiss king’s speech as road to stagnation
item.description:
Opposition parties dismiss king’s speech as road to stagnation

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Opposition parties have accused the Dutch government of failing to make choices and leading the country into a “stagnation” following a king’s speech packed with appeals to the Dutch traditions of compromise and co-operation.

In a long and wide-ranging speech, King Willem-Alexander said “communality” could be an “antidote to polarisation” and said solutions needed to be found on issues such as nitrogen pollution, the housing crisis and social unrest around asylum.

But opposition parties said the cabinet had failed to set out a clear vision or take the initiative in coming forward with ideas to fix the problems.

“Politics is about making choices,” said Joost Eerdmans, leader of the right-wing conservative JA21. “The king can say democracy isn’t 50% plus one, but that’s how it works in practice. They’ve forgotten to turn left or right, or else they can’t.”

Jesse Klaver, leader of the largest left-wing opposition party Pro, said the king’s “fine words” could not disguise the fact “that the cabinet is rudderless.”

“We are in a permanent process of forming the government because the minority government can’t agree on which way to take the country in.”

Lack of direction

In the weeks before the opening day of parliament the three coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD were unable to agree what concessions to make to opposition parties in the budget deal that finance minister Eelco Heinen will deliver on Tuesday.

Instead the minority government will have to keep negotiating with opposition leaders to find the 10 seats it needs in the lower house and the 16 seats in the Senate to pass its laws.

Mirjam Bikker, leader of the ChristenUnie, said the king’s speech showed a lack of direction from the coalition parties.

“If you want to make progress, you have to decide which way to go,” she said. “We’ve seen a few concessions on minor things like cuts to healthcare, but my concern is that without a sense of direction it’ll just be a few trinkets.”

Geert Wilders of the far-right PVV criticised the speech for failing to address people’s concerns about fundamental issues such as the rising cost of living.

”Lots of money is being spent on Europe, development aid, nitrogen and the climate, while we see the country is changing and we can’t pay the bills,” he said. ”The sooner this cabinet falls, the better.”
